name: hesiod
desc: Library for the simple string lookup service built on top of DNS
why: Hesiod is a real but obscure lookup service layered on DNS, a door into MIT-era naming, though this is only the library.

brief.what_it_is: Hesiod is a C name service library, release 3.2.1, for a simple string lookup service layered on top of DNS. A client program asks the library for a name and a type, and the library turns that into an ordinary DNS query under the configured domain. The answers are plain text records (TXT, or CNAME pointing at a TXT record) held on the central name servers. The README describes the data as general name service for a variety of applications. The Homebrew entry names one executable, hesinfo, but the README does not describe it.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says Hesiod "can provide general name service for a variety of applications" and is based on the Berkeley Internet Name Daemon (BIND). It does not give a longer motivation.
brief.how_it_works: Clients read a hesiod.conf file that sets rhs (the domain suffix) and lhs (a label, default .ns); the rhs value can be overridden by the HES_DOMAIN environment variable. Administrators make their name servers authoritative for ns.your.domain and load a zone file containing TXT records such as haynes.group and CNAME records such as 2638.gid pointing at them. A lookup therefore resolves through normal DNS to a text string.

commands_seen.context: Prepares the source directory for building; accepts options.
Alternative build target, same as make per the README.

brief.install_notes: Needs a vaguely ANSI C compiler; the README says gcc will do. Beyond building, each client machine needs a hesiod.conf in sysconfdir (default /usr/local/etc/hesiod.conf) with rhs and lhs lines, and the central DNS servers need a named.boot primary line and a named.hesiod zone file with SOA, NS and Hesiod TXT/CNAME data. The README's example uses rhs=.your.domain and lhs=.ns. No account or hardware is required.
brief.standout: It is a 1980s-style naming scheme that reuses DNS as its transport, so no new server protocol is needed; the zone data is just TXT and CNAME records. The README is candid that the .ns label is a historical accident that it would not choose today.
brief.status: Release 3.2.1 is stated in the README, but no release date or last-commit date was visible on the page I fetched. The README carries a Travis CI badge pointing at travis-ci.org, the retired legacy host, which hints the CI setup is old. Status is best described as unknown, leaning quiet.
brief.caveats: Only the library is in this package; the README mentions no client tools beyond the library itself, and the hesinfo executable named by Homebrew is not described in the README. The README assumes BIND-era named.boot configuration, which is dated. The mailing list is hesiod@mit.edu, with subscription handled through hesiod-request@mit.edu. The README is terse and gives no license text or platform list beyond the compiler note.
quotes: Hesiod can provide general name service for a variety of applications and is based on the Berkeley Internet Name Daemon (BIND).
The value ".ns" for lhs is an unfortunate historical convention; ".hs" or "hesiod" would have been better.
Hesiod requires a vaguely ANSI compiler to build; gcc will do.
fetch_log: https://github.com/achernya/hesiod - worked; GitHub README returned (release 3.2.1 text, Travis badge). No further fetches needed since the README covers build, config, and server setup.
